blocks.text: The thyroid gland is an endocrine gland situated in the anterior lower neck.

items.text: Two lobes: Right and left lobes lie on either side of the upper trachea.
Isthmus: Connects the two lobes, usually over the second to fourth tracheal rings.
Pyramidal lobe: An occasional superior extension, usually arising from the isthmus or adjacent lobe.
Capsule: The gland is enclosed by connective tissue and is attached to the larynx and trachea, explaining why it normally moves during swallowing.
Blood supply: Principally from the superior and inferior thyroid arteries.

blocks.text: Important surface landmarks:

rows: The prominent laryngeal prominence, often called the Adam's apple
Usually lies below the cricoid cartilage
Helps assess lower thyroid enlargement and possible retrosternal extension

blocks.text: Key examination principle: A thyroid swelling typically moves upwards with swallowing because the gland is attached to the larynx. A swelling arising from another structure may behave differently.

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the examination and obtain consent.
Ask whether the patient has neck pain or tenderness.
Ask permission to expose the neck from the chin to the upper chest, maintaining dignity.
Position the patient sitting upright, with the neck slightly flexed to relax the sternocleidomastoid muscles.
Stand in front of the patient for initial inspection and usually move behind the patient for palpation.
Ensure adequate lighting.

blocks.text: Equipment: A stethoscope, measuring tape if required, and a penlight or examination light when appropriate.
In an OSCE, tell the examiner that you would also measure the patient's vital signs and assess for signs of thyroid dysfunction.
Although this is a physical examination station, a brief focused history helps you interpret your findings.

rows: Haemorrhage into a nodule, inflammation or malignancy
Difficulty breathing, especially when lying flat
Laryngeal nerve involvement or another laryngeal disorder
Palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, weight loss
Cold intolerance, constipation, fatigue, weight gain
Previous thyroid disease, surgery or neck irradiation
Recurrence, altered anatomy or malignancy risk
Family history of thyroid disease or thyroid cancer
Medication use, including amiodarone, lithium and thyroid medication

blocks.text: Urgent red flags: Stridor, significant breathing difficulty, rapidly expanding neck swelling, or new hoarseness with a suspicious thyroid mass require urgent assessment.
Stand in front of the patient. Inspect the neck at rest and while the patient swallows.
Observe the following systematically.
1. General neck symmetry

items.text: Normal: No visible anterior neck swelling; the neck is symmetrical.
Abnormal: Anterior neck swelling, unilateral enlargement, asymmetry or a visible thyroid nodule.

blocks.text: 2. Position and extent of swelling
Determine whether a swelling is in the lower anterior neck and whether it is central or lateral.

items.text: Diffuse enlargement suggests conditions such as Graves disease, iodine deficiency or Hashimoto thyroiditis.
A solitary swelling may represent a thyroid nodule or cyst.
Multiple nodules suggest multinodular goitre.
A large lower-neck swelling may extend behind the sternum.

blocks.text: Remember that not every anterior neck swelling is thyroid in origin. Consider lymph nodes, thyroglossal duct cysts, other neck masses and laryngeal abnormalities.
3. Skin overlying the gland

items.text: Normal: Skin appears normal, without erythema, scars or dilated veins.
Abnormal: Redness, scars from previous surgery, prominent superficial veins or skin tethering.

blocks.text: Skin fixation, ulceration or other invasive features are concerning, particularly when associated with a hard thyroid mass.
4. Visible pulsation

items.text: Normal: No abnormal pulsation.
Abnormal: Prominent pulsation may occur in a highly vascular gland, including Graves disease, but is not diagnostic on its own.

blocks.text: 5. Tracheal position
Look at the trachea and the midline of the neck for apparent deviation.

items.text: Normal: Trachea appears central.
Abnormal: Tracheal deviation may result from a large thyroid mass or another neck or mediastinal lesion.

blocks.text: Confirm suspected deviation by palpation.

content_groups.group_title: B. Ask the patient to swallow

blocks.text: Ask the patient to take a sip of water and swallow while you observe the neck.

items.text: Normal: The thyroid may not be visibly apparent, but the gland moves upwards with swallowing if appreciable.
Abnormal: A visible thyroid swelling rises with swallowing, supporting a thyroid origin.

blocks.text: A mass that does not move normally may be adherent to surrounding structures, although movement alone cannot establish or exclude its origin.
Examiner question: Why does the thyroid move on swallowing?
Because the gland is enclosed by pretracheal fascia and attached to the laryngeal framework, it moves upwards as the larynx elevates during swallowing.

content_groups.group_title: C. Ask the patient to protrude the tongue if indicated

blocks.text: This is not a routine test for thyroid enlargement, but it is useful when distinguishing a suspected thyroglossal duct cyst from a thyroid swelling.

items.text: A thyroglossal duct cyst typically moves upwards with both swallowing and tongue protrusion.
A thyroid swelling typically moves with swallowing but not specifically with tongue protrusion.

blocks.text: Neither sign is perfectly diagnostic.
Palpation is one of the most important parts of the examination. It establishes the gland's size, consistency, surface, tenderness, nodularity, mobility and relationship to surrounding structures.
Stand behind the seated patient. Ask them to relax their neck and flex their chin slightly downwards.
Place your fingers gently over the lower anterior neck, with your fingers around the region of the thyroid gland.
Identify the thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage and trachea before assessing the gland.
Identify the isthmus over the upper trachea, just below the cricoid cartilage.

items.text: Normal: It may be difficult to feel and is not enlarged.
Abnormal: A thickened or nodular isthmus may indicate thyroid enlargement or nodular disease.

blocks.text: Ask the patient to swallow and feel the gland move beneath your fingers.

content_groups.group_title: Step 3: Palpate the right and left lobes

blocks.text: Displace the trachea gently to one side, where appropriate, to bring the opposite lobe into better reach. Palpate each lobe systematically, then repeat on the other side.
Assess each lobe for the following six features.
1. Size

items.text: Normal: No palpable enlargement or a gland within expected normal limits.
Abnormal: Diffuse enlargement, unilateral enlargement, or a discrete nodule.

blocks.text: 2. Surface

items.text: Normal: Smooth.
Abnormal: Nodular or irregular, as in multinodular goitre or a thyroid lesion.

blocks.text: 3. Consistency

items.text: Normal: Soft to firm, depending on the individual.
Abnormal: Very firm, hard or irregular. A hard nodule is concerning for malignancy, although benign lesions can also be firm.

blocks.text: 4. Tenderness

items.text: Normal: Non-tender.
Abnormal: Tenderness may suggest subacute thyroiditis, acute inflammation or haemorrhage into a nodule.

blocks.text: 5. Nodules

items.text: Normal: No discrete nodules.
Abnormal: Record the number, location, approximate size, consistency, tenderness and mobility of each palpable nodule.

blocks.text: 6. Mobility and fixation

items.text: Normal: The gland moves upwards with swallowing and is not fixed to surrounding tissues.
Abnormal: Reduced mobility or fixation raises concern for invasive disease, fibrosis or other pathology.

blocks.text: Try to palpate the inferior border of each lobe.

items.text: Normal: The lower border is accessible.
Abnormal: The inferior border cannot be reached, especially in a large goitre.

blocks.text: An impalpable lower border raises suspicion of retrosternal extension but does not prove it. Further assessment, often with imaging, may be required.

content_groups.group_title: Step 5: Assess the gland during swallowing

blocks.text: Ask the patient to swallow water again while palpating the gland.

items.text: Normal: The gland moves upwards freely.
Abnormal: Restricted movement, fixation or an asymmetrical mass may warrant further investigation.

content_groups.group_title: Step 6: Assess for fluctuation where appropriate

blocks.text: If a lesion feels cystic, assess its consistency and whether it is fluctuant, using gentle technique.
A fluctuant nodule may represent a thyroid cyst, but palpation cannot reliably distinguish a benign cyst from other thyroid lesions.

content_groups.group_title: How to describe a palpable thyroid swelling

blocks.text: Use this sequence:
Site → size → surface → consistency → tenderness → nodules → mobility → lower border → tracheal position.
For example:

“There is a diffuse, symmetrical enlargement of the thyroid gland involving both lobes and the isthmus. The gland is smooth, firm, non-tender and moves upwards with swallowing. No discrete nodules are palpable, and the lower border is accessible.”
That is a structured description of a diffuse goitre. It does not, by itself, establish the cause or thyroid functional status.
medistudents.com
Auscultation is particularly important when the thyroid is enlarged or Graves disease is suspected.

items.text: Ask the patient to remain seated and relaxed.
Place the diaphragm of the stethoscope gently over each thyroid lobe.
Listen over both lobes, and over a prominent nodule if appropriate.
Compare the two sides.
Normal: No bruit is heard.
Abnormal: A thyroid bruit is a blowing vascular sound heard over the gland.

blocks.text: A bruit may occur in Graves disease because of increased vascularity and blood flow. It can also occur in other hypervascular thyroid conditions.
Clinical distinction: A bruit is a sound produced by turbulent blood flow. It is not the same as a palpable thrill, which is a vibration felt with the fingers.
A large goitre may extend into the superior mediastinum, where it can compress the trachea or other structures.

items.text: A large swelling in the lower neck.
Dyspnoea, especially when supine.
Dysphagia.
Stridor or noisy breathing.
Venous congestion in the neck or upper chest.

blocks.text: Percuss over the upper sternum if retrosternal extension is suspected.

items.text: Normal: Resonance over the underlying air-containing lung regions, as appropriate to the area examined.
Abnormal: Dullness over the manubrium may raise suspicion of a retrosternal mass, but this is not sensitive or specific.

blocks.text: medizzy.com
Ask the patient to raise both arms above their head, if safe, and observe the face and neck for up to a minute.

items.text: Negative: No facial plethora, cyanosis, respiratory distress or venous congestion develops.
Positive: Facial flushing or plethora, cyanosis, neck vein distension, or respiratory difficulty develops.

blocks.text: A positive Pemberton's sign suggests thoracic inlet obstruction, which may be caused by a retrosternal goitre.

Safety: Stop immediately if the patient develops breathlessness, stridor, dizziness or significant distress. Do not perform this manoeuvre in an unstable patient or when severe airway compression is already suspected.

subsections.subsection_title: 8. Examination of the cervical lymph nodes

blocks.text: Thyroid examination is incomplete without examining the cervical lymph nodes, particularly when a thyroid nodule or suspicious mass is present.
intechopen.com

blocks.title: Stand behind or in front of the patient and palpate systematically:

items.text: Submental nodes.
Submandibular nodes.
Preauricular and postauricular nodes.
Occipital nodes.
Tonsillar or jugulodigastric nodes.
Superficial cervical nodes.
Deep cervical chain.
Posterior cervical nodes.
Supraclavicular nodes.

blocks.title: For any palpable node, describe its:

items.text: Site and number.
Size.
Tenderness.
Consistency.
Mobility or fixation.
Matting, if present.

rows: Concerning for malignant or granulomatous disease
Enlarged cervical nodes with a thyroid nodule
Raises concern for thyroid malignancy, depending on the clinical context
Requires careful assessment for significant underlying disease

blocks.text: Not every enlarged lymph node in a patient with thyroid disease is caused by the thyroid.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Assess for signs of thyroid dysfunction

blocks.text: A thyroid gland can be enlarged while producing normal amounts of thyroid hormone. Conversely, a patient can have thyroid dysfunction without a palpable goitre.
Therefore, you must assess the patient's thyroid status, not just the gland.

items.text: Warm, moist palms — may occur in thyrotoxicosis.
Fine tremor — ask the patient to extend their arms, spread their fingers and extend their wrists; place a sheet of paper over the fingers if necessary.
Palmar erythema.
Onycholysis, or separation of the nail from the nail bed, particularly in thyrotoxicosis.
Thyroid acropachy — rare clubbing-like changes associated with Graves disease.

blocks.text: Assess the radial pulse for rate, rhythm and character.

rows: Supports thyrotoxicosis in the appropriate context

blocks.text: Do not diagnose thyroid disease from any single finding.

items.text: Exophthalmos or proptosis.
Lid retraction.
Lid lag.
Periorbital swelling.
Conjunctival redness or chemosis.
Restricted extraocular movements.
Reduced visual acuity or colour vision if orbital disease is suspected.

blocks.text: Graves orbitopathy may cause proptosis, lid retraction and diplopia. These features are not present in every patient with Graves disease.

Important distinction: Lid lag is delayed downward movement of the upper eyelid when the patient follows a moving object downwards. Lid retraction is an abnormally high resting position of the upper eyelid.
Look for additional features:
Possible thyrotoxicosis

items.text: Weight loss despite normal or increased appetite.
Heat intolerance and sweating.
Anxiety or restlessness.
Proximal muscle weakness.
Hyperreflexia.
Increased bowel frequency.

blocks.text: Possible hypothyroidism

items.text: Weight gain.
Cold intolerance.
Dry skin and coarse hair.
Facial puffiness.
Hoarse voice.
Constipation.
Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes.

blocks.text: Other important findings

items.text: Pretibial myxoedema, particularly in Graves disease.
Proximal myopathy.
Signs of heart failure or arrhythmia.
Menstrual disturbance, where relevant to the history.

blocks.text: For a complete OSCE, examine the cardiovascular system and perform a focused neurological examination when indicated.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Clinical patterns: what different thyroid findings suggest

blocks.text: Diffuse toxic goitre
A diffusely enlarged, usually smooth gland, with possible bruit, tremor, tachycardia and eye signs.
Consider Graves disease; confirm thyroid function and investigate the cause.
Multinodular goitre
An irregular or nodular enlarged gland, often with multiple palpable nodules.
Thyroid function may be normal, increased or decreased.
Hashimoto thyroiditis
The gland may be diffusely enlarged, firm and non-tender, with features of hypothyroidism in some patients.
Confirm with thyroid function tests and, when appropriate, thyroid antibodies.
Subacute thyroiditis
A tender thyroid, often with anterior neck pain that may radiate towards the jaw or ears.
Thyroid function can change over the course of the illness.
Solitary thyroid nodule
A discrete lump within one lobe, which may be smooth or irregular, soft or hard.
Most nodules are benign, but suspicious features require investigation.

content_groups.group_title: Features that raise concern for thyroid malignancy

items.text: A hard, irregular thyroid nodule.
Fixation to surrounding structures.
Persistent or progressive hoarseness.
Enlarged suspicious cervical lymph nodes.
Rapid growth, particularly when accompanied by other suspicious findings.
A history of childhood head or neck irradiation.
A strong family history of thyroid cancer or relevant hereditary cancer syndromes.

blocks.text: These are warning signs, not definitive proof of cancer. Some malignant nodules are mobile and painless, while some benign lesions are firm.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Investigations you should know for the examination

blocks.text: An OSCE examiner may ask: “You have found a thyroid nodule. What would you do next?”
A structured answer is to assess thyroid function, characterize the nodule, and determine whether malignancy or compression is suspected.

rows: Free T4, with free T3 when indicated
Assesses gland size, nodules, suspicious features and cervical lymph nodes
Evaluates nodules meeting appropriate clinical and ultrasound criteria
Supports evaluation for autoimmune thyroid disease when indicated
May help assess a nodule when TSH is suppressed, subject to pregnancy and other contraindications
May be required to assess retrosternal extension or compression
May be indicated for persistent hoarseness, vocal cord dysfunction or suspected laryngeal nerve involvement

blocks.text: Key exam point: Ultrasound risk features and clinical context guide whether FNA is indicated; not every thyroid nodule requires biopsy. TSH is generally the initial thyroid function test, with further testing guided by the result and clinical suspicion.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. How to present normal thyroid findings

blocks.text: In an OSCE, present your findings in a concise, organized sequence.
Normal findings — sample presentation

“On examination of the neck, there is no visible thyroid enlargement or asymmetry. The thyroid gland is not enlarged on palpation, is non-tender, and no discrete nodules are palpable. There is no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The trachea is central, and no thyroid bruit is audible. There are no obvious clinical features of thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism.”
Copy normal presentation
Only report that the gland is non-enlarged if your examination supports that conclusion. Do not state that the thyroid function is normal based on physical examination alone.
The following are sample presentations. Adapt them to what you actually find.
A. Diffuse goitre

“There is a diffuse, symmetrical enlargement of the thyroid gland involving both lobes and the isthmus. The gland is smooth, firm, non-tender and moves upwards with swallowing. No discrete nodules are palpable. The trachea is central, and no cervical lymphadenopathy or thyroid bruit is detected.”
Interpretation: Diffuse goitre; the cause and thyroid functional status require further assessment.
Copy presentation
B. Multinodular goitre

“The thyroid gland is enlarged, with an irregular nodular surface involving both lobes. Multiple nodules of varying sizes are palpable. The gland moves with swallowing. I would assess the tracheal position, lower border, cervical lymph nodes and signs of thyroid dysfunction.”
Interpretation: Multinodular goitre; thyroid function and ultrasound findings will guide further investigation.
Copy presentation
C. Solitary thyroid nodule

“There is a discrete nodule in the right thyroid lobe, approximately [size] cm in diameter. It is [consistency], [tender/non-tender], and [mobile/restricted] on swallowing. I would assess the remaining gland, cervical lymph nodes, tracheal position and signs of thyroid dysfunction.”
Interpretation: Solitary thyroid nodule requiring appropriate clinical, biochemical and ultrasound assessment.
Copy presentation
D. Suspicious thyroid mass

“There is an enlarged thyroid gland with a hard, irregular nodule that appears fixed to surrounding structures. There is associated [site and description of lymph nodes, if present]. These findings are concerning for possible thyroid malignancy and warrant urgent specialist assessment.”
Interpretation: Suspicious clinical features; malignancy cannot be confirmed by examination alone.
Copy presentation

subsections.subsection_title: 14. OSCE checklist: do not miss these steps

blocks.text: 0 of 14
Introduce yourself, explain the examination and obtain consent
Position the patient and expose the neck appropriately
Inspect the neck at rest
Observe the gland during swallowing
Palpate the isthmus and both lobes
Assess size, surface, consistency, tenderness and nodules
Assess mobility and palpate the lower border
Check tracheal position
Auscultate for a thyroid bruit when indicated
Examine cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes
Assess hands, tremor, pulse and eyes for thyroid dysfunction
Look for signs of retrosternal extension and compression
Thank the patient, cover them and wash your hands
Summarize findings and suggest appropriate further investigations
1. Why does a thyroid swelling move with swallowing?
Because it is attached to the laryngeal framework through the surrounding fascia and moves upwards when the larynx elevates.
2. What does a thyroid bruit suggest?
Increased vascularity and turbulent blood flow, classically seen in Graves disease.
3. What does an impalpable lower border suggest?
Possible retrosternal extension, although further assessment is required to confirm it.
4. How do you differentiate a thyroid swelling from a thyroglossal duct cyst?
Both can move with swallowing. A thyroglossal duct cyst typically also moves with tongue protrusion.
5. Can a patient have a normal thyroid examination but abnormal thyroid function?
Yes. Thyroid dysfunction can occur without visible or palpable enlargement.
6. What are the most concerning findings in a thyroid nodule?
Fixation, hardness, suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy, progressive growth, persistent hoarseness and relevant risk factors.
7. What is the first-line blood test for thyroid function?
TSH is generally the initial test, followed by free T4 and, when indicated, free T3.
8. What is the difference between a goitre and thyrotoxicosis?
A goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland. Thyrotoxicosis is the clinical and biochemical state caused by excessive thyroid hormone action. A patient can have either condition without the other.

blocks.title: Always separate your conclusions into three questions:

items.text: Is the gland enlarged or nodular? — Answered primarily by inspection and palpation.
Is the gland causing compression or showing features concerning for malignancy? — Answered through examination of the gland, trachea, lymph nodes and relevant symptoms.
Is the patient euthyroid, hyperthyroid or hypothyroid? — Requires clinical assessment and appropriate thyroid function tests.

blocks.text: That distinction is essential in clinical examinations and real patient care.
